sentences.text: Romerodus is classified as a holocephalan, a group of cartilaginous fish today represented only by chimaeras, placing it distantly related to living relatives within the class Chondrichthyes.

Most of its cartilaginous skeleton was calcified, except for the vertebral centra and dorsal fin radials, with a single dorsal fin supported by fused basal cartilage positioned above the pectoral girdle.
The animal possessed broad, flattened, overlapping pavement-like teeth, including a distinctive whorl of teeth along the midline of the lower jaw that spanned about 25% of the skull's length.
The largest known Romerodus reached approximately 50 cm in total length.
A specimen of indeterminate species in the René Kindlimann collection measures 56 cm in length.

Scaling Romerodus's proportions suggests the largest Helicoprion individuals may have reached 7 to 11 meters in length, a hypothesis used to model a life-sized replica at the Idaho Museum of Natural History.
The genus Romerodus was named by Rainer Zangerl in 1981, with the type species Romerodus orodontus described from multiple crushed but well-preserved body fossils.
All described specimens come from the Hansen Quarry in Sarpy County, Nebraska, where the incomplete articulated specimen FMNH PF 8522 from the Stark Shale serves as the holotype.
Isolated teeth possibly belonging to Romerodus have also been found in the Early Permian Phosphoria Formation in Grand Teton and Yellowstone national parks.
Romerodus lived in deep marine waters and is considered an active, nektonic carnivore and a very powerful swimmer adapted as a pelagic predator.
Its anatomy indicates it was an active, nektonic carnivore capable of powerful swimming.
Romerodus belongs to the family Caseodontidae.
Romerodus fossils date to the Pennsylvanian subperiod and possibly the Early Permian, living during the Kasimovian stage between 307 and 303.7 million years ago in North America.

Fossils from the type specimen were found in the Stark Shale, a marine depositional environment formed when the area was part of the Late Pennsylvanian Midcontinent Sea, a deep inland sea rich in phosphates and organic material.
It is debated whether eugeneodonts' shark-like morphology was due to shared ecology rather than direct ancestry with sharks.
